common_name: Moonlight Japanese Hydrangea Vine (Silvery-Blue Variegated Climbing Vine)

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring against a shaded wall, tree trunk, or sturdy trellis in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil.

directions: Moonlight is prized less for its flowers than for its striking heart-shaped leaves, which are heavily overlaid with silvery-blue pewter tones between prominent dark green veins, giving the whole plant a frosted, almost metallic sheen in shaded conditions. It attaches itself to masonry, bark, and trellis wire using aerial rootlets and needs no tying or training once it gains a foothold, though like most Schizophragma it can sulk for a couple of seasons before putting on real growth. Foliage color develops best with a few hours of dappled or morning sun rather than deep, dense shade. Prune only to control size or remove dead wood, ideally right after the creamy midsummer bracts fade, since flowers form on old wood.
sources: Great Plant Picks (Elisabeth C. Miller Botanical Garden)

common_name: Roseum Japanese Hydrangea Vine (Pink-Bracted Climbing Vine)

planting.note: Set out container-grown plants in spring at the base of a shaded wall or mature tree in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil.

directions: Roseum is a long-sought selection of Japanese hydrangea vine grown for its solitary enlarged bracts, which emerge blush-white and deepen to a soft rose-pink as the lacecap-style flower heads mature in midsummer, giving the whole vine a warmer glow than the species. Growth habit mirrors the straight species: it climbs by clinging aerial rootlets, needs no wires or trellis once established, and typically takes two to three seasons to root in before vigorous vertical growth begins. Best bract color and density develop where the vine gets a few hours of gentle morning light rather than year-round dense shade. Keep the root zone consistently moist and mulched, and limit pruning to shaping right after flowering.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database
American Horticultural Society — A-Z Encyclopedia of Garden Plants

subcategory: non-native climbing vine (invasive, regulated in parts of eastern US)

planting.note: Before planting, confirm this species is legal in your state — it is banned or regulated as invasive in Connecticut, Massachusetts, New Hampshire, and Vermont, among other jurisdictions.

directions: This vigorous Asian vine is grown chiefly for its ornamental berries, which ripen through a striking sequence of lilac, turquoise, and cobalt on the same cluster in late summer, but it readily escapes cultivation and outcompetes native vegetation in disturbed woodland edges, riverbanks, and hedgerows across the eastern and midwestern United States. It tolerates deep shade to full sun and average to poor soils, which is precisely why it spreads so aggressively once established, and birds distribute the seed widely. Given its regulated or banned status in several states, gardeners should strongly consider native alternatives such as Parthenocissus quinquefolia or Ampelopsis cordata instead, which fill a similar ecological niche without the invasive risk. Where it remains legal to grow, keep it confined to a container or hard-pruned trellis, remove flowers before they set fruit, and monitor surrounding areas closely for seedlings.
sources: USDA Forest Service — Weed of the Week: Porcelain-berry
Invasive Plant Atlas of the United States
University of Connecticut Extension — invasive plant list

planting.note: Set out container-grown plants in spring once soil has warmed, giving roots a season to establish before the first winter test of their cold tolerance.

directions: Selected for noticeably greater cold hardiness than the straight species, this cultivar shrugs off brief dips into the low teens with only minor leaf burn, resprouting reliably where standard star jasmine would suffer dieback. Grow it on a trellis, arbor, or fence in part shade to full sun with fertile, well-drained soil, and expect the same glossy dark foliage and intensely fragrant white pinwheel blooms in late spring through early summer. Keep soil evenly moist while young, then taper watering once established, and prune lightly after the flowering flush to keep twining stems in bounds. In colder pockets of its range it can also be grown as a low, dense groundcover if left unstaked and sheared periodically.
